extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimentalists, and students studying the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for planning, conducting, and interpreting experiments across the sciences, emphasizing controls, measurement, and the move from qualitative detection to quantitative laws. Covers practical precautions (blind trials, calibration, visualization), limits of experiment, and methods of variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind (test) experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Every conclusive experiment necessarily consists in the comparison of results between two different combinations of circumstances. Blind experiments — trying whether an effect appears in the absence of the suspected cause — are an essential part of any experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a blind trial whenever possible to avoid assuming the outcome (examples: Marsh's test for arsenic; Faraday examining bearing apparatus in absence of the test substance). Anti-pattern: omitting a blind test and thereby assuming one 'knows' what would happen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and validation by introducing known amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the accuracy of a method by introducing known amounts of the substance or force to be detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate new analytical processes by performing them on mixtures containing known quantities (examples: assay gold by assaying alloys of exactly known composition; try a divining rod in places where veins of metal are known). Use known standards or 'spikes' to assess accuracy and recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret negative results with caution (detection limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of instrument imperfection and possible minuteness of effects, negative experimental results must be interpreted cautiously; a single experiment cannot prove non-existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sensitivity and possible confounding effects (examples: Bennet's failure to detect momentum of light vs Crookes' later detection; inability to prove the moon has no atmosphere). To conclude non-existence, demonstrate deductively that an effect, if present, would have been perceptible given the methods used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of experiment (time scales and inimitable processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many natural operations cannot be imitated in experiment (e.g., processes requiring enormous time or scale), so experimental scope is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissing long-term or large-scale natural phenomena because they don't appear within historical experiment durations (examples: geological change, origin of species). Be careful when extrapolating short-term experiments to geological or evolutionary timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress from qualitative detection to quantitative inquiry (method of variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with qualitative (existence) experiments; once an effect is shown to be discoverable, proceed to quantitative inquiries to determine how the effect varies with conditions and to express laws mathematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative induction seeks functions or equations relating conditions and effects; the method of variation (varying one quantity and measuring the variant) is the general application of experiment to continuously variable phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and control the variable and the variant
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the variable (the antecedent under the experimenter's control) and the variant (the measured consequent), and ensure the variable is under command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the antecedent quantity to vary (examples: heat/temperature as variable, length as variant in thermal expansion). If the variable cannot be governed (capricious forces), accurate measurement becomes difficult and results less useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain a regular, governable supply of the variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where natural sources vary, create uniform and controllable sources of the variable so experiments can be performed under stable, measurable conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Smeaton moving windmill models on a revolving arm to produce uniform wind; use steady artificial light sources instead of the sun; Fizeau/Wheatstone methods to measure light velocity in controlled settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure variables and conditions with comparable accuracy; define conditions precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact measurement of an effect is of little use unless the experimental conditions can also be exactly defined and measured; measurement accuracy should be appropriate to the definability of conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't measure to an accuracy that exceeds your ability to fix the object's conditions (examples: variable forms of carbon; boiling point dependence on impurities/air; meteorological measures influenced by transient sky conditions). Ensure condition definitions are repeatable for future reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain similar conditions; control confounding factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To attribute cause to a single condition, keep all surrounding conditions constant except the one being studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match preparations, shapes, magnitudes (Gilbert: 'similar preparation, similar figure, and of equal magnitude'). Examples: Newton's pendulum experiment matched boxes/threads/weights so air resistance and geometry were the same; Joule's apparatus compared separated vs connected vessels to isolate energy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design simple, isolated changes to reveal causal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A single deliberate change in apparatus or procedure can produce indications of the utmost significance and clarify causal relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep changes minimal and interpretable (example: Joule's single change of separating water baths revealed relation of mechanical work and heat). The art of experiment often lies in simple, decisive modifications rather than complex alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use collective experiments / collective instances for simultaneous observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective experiments present a continuous range or many quantitative results at once (e.g., wedge-shaped cells, inclined plates) allowing observation of many cases in a single setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for initial discovery, visualization, and sometimes precise measurement when patterns are stable (examples: wedge glass showing progressive absorption; Newton's rings and diffraction fringes permitting accurate measurement). Generally good for illustration and hypothesis generation; may be less precise for exact measurement unless the collective curve is permanent and measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render invisible motions and structures visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visualization techniques (smoke, powders, reagents) to make the motions of gases or liquids or other otherwise invisible phenomena observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: smoke to show air movements; lycopodium powder in liquids; spreading dilute reagents (salt and silver nitrate) to produce visible clouds at interfaces; iron filings to depict magnetic lines of force. Visualization aids comprehension and suggests quantitative follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for periodic versus secular (non-periodic) variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish periodic phenomena (which return to the same value as the variable, e.g., time, progresses) from secular variations (steady changes without return), and treat them accordingly in experimental design and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pendulum oscillations and orbital motions are periodic; a body projected into free space shows secular motion. Recognize periodicity when analysing variation and when applying the method of variations.
